summary: This collection of early modern Latin poetry by Michael Abel consists of 'Carminum' (odes) and 'Elegiarum' (elegies). The work is organized into twenty sections featuring a blend of devotional, pastoral, and occasional poetry. It contains meditations on Christology, the Passion, the Eucharist, and the life of the saints, alongside classical themes involving Apollo, Venus, the Muses, and the Hesperides. The text includes specific dedications to figures such as Maximilian II, the Duke of Savoy, Andreas Ebersdorffer, and Johannes Sambucus. Geographical references include Dresden, Vienna, Assisi, the Ister (Danube), and the city of Thebes. Additional subjects include medical descriptions of podagra and thermal springs, a polemic against Muhammad, and reflections on the sacrifice of Abel.

This collection of Latin poems and epigrams includes a dedication to the reader, a defense of the author's poetic style, and several themed sections. The texts address religious themes such as the 'Crown of Piety,' the 'Vocation of the Nations' to Christ, and the 'Icon of Christ the Patient,' alongside more classical and allegorical subjects like the 'Poets' (Helicon), the 'Night of the Messiah's Birth,' and a meditation on the passage of time and mortality.

This section of the Latin poetry contains a series of short, often allegorical or moralizing stanzas and fragments. It includes references to Christ, the Muses, and the figure of Adam, alongside mythological and geographical references such as the Styx, the Syrtes, and the underworld (Orcus). The text features several headings or titles in capital letters, such as 'CALLIMACHI', 'IN IMAGINE MICHAELIS', and 'MORSUS POMI LETHALIS', and contains a series of prayers or petitions to God.

This section of Michael Abel's poetry contains a series of short lyrical and devotional poems. It includes a meditation on the Passion of Christ (IN CRUCEM REDEMPTORIS), a biblical reflection on the sacrifice of Abel (DE ABELE), a poem on the birth of Christ (TEMPUS FILII DEI natale), and a reflection on the conversion of Saul (DE SAULE R.).

This section of the collection contains a series of poems and hymns including a psalm, a prayer by a monk named Nicolaus, and a piece titled 'In Novum Annum'. The texts address themes of divine judgment, the suffering of the Church, the fall of man, and the nature of sin. Specific references are made to figures such as Serapis, the serpent of the Styx, and the city of Babylon.

This section of the collection contains several poems and inscriptions with varied themes: the spiritual and physical properties of wine (Vineyard of the Church, Wine from Water), the figure of Ganymede, and a reflection on the fate of a poet. It also includes a religious meditation on the Resurrection (Day of Easter), a critique of Pharisaic hypocrisy, and a concluding poem on the fortunes of a figure named Pericleus.

This section contains a collection of short Latin poems and inscriptions including a pastoral scene in a garden, a lament for a friend, a Christological meditation, and a tribute to Saint Bartholomew. It also includes a satirical piece on 'assentators' (likely a reference to those who agree to things without thinking), a reflection on the passage of time, and a concluding meditation on the afterlife.

This section contains a series of short poems and meditations on religious and mythological themes. It includes a plea to the elements (Borea, Frigora) for safe passage, a lament for the lack of fruit addressed to Ceres, and a narrative regarding the birth of a king and the actions of Herod. The text also features a tribute to a friend, a reference to the city of Assisi, and a concluding section based on Psalm 117 (Psalm 116 in modern numbering).

This collection of poems and fragments includes a series of religious hymns praising the goodness and mercy of God, a section on music and its relation to the soul, and a series of shorter poems on themes of parsimony, nature, and fate. The text includes specific references to the figures of Achilles, Venus, and the poet Simiolos, as well as a personal address to a friend and a critique of a poet named Philip.

This section contains a series of short poems and epigrams including a lament for a lost legacy, a description of a squirrel navigating a timber ridge, and a formal invocation to the Muses. It includes a religious section on Saint Peter (Divus Petrus) and a brief narrative regarding the flight of the Messiah into Egypt.

This section contains a series of religious and poetic fragments, including a hymn to Christ, a meditation on the Easter lamb, and a passage on the illness of King Hezekiah. It includes an epitaph for a mathematician named Valentinus Engelhart and a concluding section regarding pagan idols and the worship of Jupiter.

This section of the poems contains a series of short, often cryptic, lyrical and religious fragments. It includes a poem addressed to a friend regarding the vanity of seeking fortune in the stars, a reflection on the nature of death and resurrection (Vita ex Obitu), and several brief meditations on the divine word, the seasons, and the endurance of faith.

This section contains a series of poems and epitaphs, including a lament on mortality, a dedication to a friend, and a commemorative piece for the year 1787. It features specific dedications and mentions of figures such as Christ, Moses, Elijah, and a woman named Ranzovia. The text includes a formal epitaph and a concluding piece for a patron.

This section contains a series of short Latin poems and inscriptions, including a dedication to Emperor Maximilian II and a reference to Emperor Rudolph II. The texts feature mythological and allegorical imagery involving figures like Juno, Apollo (Phaebus), and various deities, alongside descriptions of natural phenomena like rain and storms. Specific locations mentioned include Dresden and a reference to the 'Imperial Aquila' and the Austrian lineage.

This section contains a series of occasional poems and dedications including a tribute to a fountain (Tiliam Dresensem), a wedding song (In Easdem Nuptias), and a celebratory hymn to the Emperor (Hymenaeus). It includes specific dedications to individuals such as Zachariae Prantelio and a commemorative verse for the death of King Louis of Hungary (Ludovicus). The text also features mythological references to figures like Leucothea, Venus, and Daphne, and a description of a garden (Hortus Caesarium).

This section contains a collection of short poems and dedications. It includes a poem about the siege of a Pannonian castle by the Turks, a dedication to a prefect of Vienna (D. Hugonem Bloti), a poem about a poet named Haslobius, and several shorter pieces including a lament for a girl named Margaris, a poem on the theme of 'Convivium', and a poem dedicated to a woman named Bigeri.

This section contains a collection of diverse Latin texts including lyrical verses on beauty and mythology, a funeral epitaph for Count Christian of Oldenburg, and several shorter poems or inscriptions. Specific subjects include the figures of Pallas, Icarus, and the deityes of the Heliconian forest, as well as a satirical piece regarding a scholar's lack of temperance and a warning against mixing absinthe with wine.

This section contains a series of short poems and dedications, including a poem on friendship (De Amicitia), a dedication to the Duke of Savoy (Duci Sabaudiae) mentioning Emanuel Philibert, and a poem addressed to Apollo (De Bruma ad Apollinem). It includes a satirical or allegorical piece regarding the Emperor Domitian and a tribute to a physician named Boaeus, concluding with a laudatory entry for Lucas Coceii Halecens.

This section contains a series of poetic fragments and dedications, including a passage titled 'TRITON HASLOBIANUS' and a section 'DE EODEM' featuring a figure named Triton Haslobianus. It includes a religious and polemical passage regarding the 'execution of the hearts' of those who 'shed the blood of Christians,' a section titled 'PALAE TRANSVERSAE Caspar' involving a character named Caspar, and a concluding section 'DE PINDARIS SENTENTIA'.

This section contains a series of short poems and dedications including an 'In Aemulum', a 'Amico Deficienti', an 'Epicedii Commendatio', a 'De Adolescente Naivo', and a 'De Angelis'. The texts address themes of artistic merit, the physical and spiritual resurrection of Christ, the defense of the faith against skepticism (specifically addressing a 'Thomas'), and a concluding invocation of the Muses and the Camenae.

This section contains a series of dedicatory poems and celebratory verses. It includes a dedication to the 'lunary' poems of the 'Eclipse of the Moon' to a priest named Clius, and a lengthy panegyric to Ioann Myller of Prague, praising his wit, literary skill, and role as an arbiter of jokes. The text also includes a dedication to a friend named Huccus and mentions various mythological figures such as Minerva, Apollo, and the Muses.

This section of the poem contains a series of addresses to two specific individuals: Andreas Ebersdorffer, a physician from Vienna, and a woman from Lidel (referred to as the 'gemmula patriae Lideli'). The text includes a formal dedication to both, a discussion of their shared virtues and 'sacred' friendship, and a series of poetic invocations involving mythological figures like Apollo, Juno, and Venus. The passage concludes with a final dedication to a friend.

The text contains a series of Latin poems and dedications. It includes a personal reflection on the influence of Martin Luther's doctrine and a dedication to Carolus Utenhovius. The latter section features a formal address to a poet, discussing themes of literary art, the study of sacred mysteries, and the interpretation of complex figures and symbols.

This section contains a series of panegyrics and dedications addressed to various figures, including a poet/historian identified as Sambucus (Johannes Sambucus) and a figure associated with the name 'Praestus'. The text includes a dedication to 'D. IOHANNEM SAMBUCUM Pannonium' and references to the Muses, the river Ister, and the city of Thebes. It also contains a brief, seemingly unrelated passage regarding 'ISMAELIS FABRICII' and the Hebrew people.

This section contains a series of Latin poems and dedications, including a tribute to D. Hugoni Blotius and a memorial for Oswaldus Scriba of Nivimontum. It features a celebratory poem for the Kalends of January (Kalendae Ianuariae) and a dedication to Carolus Nucellius. The text mentions several figures and locations, including Vienna, the Ister (Danube) river, and references to classical figures like Apollo and Juno.

The text contains a series of poetic addresses and dedications involving figures such as Lideli, Prideni, and the poet Ebersdorffus. It features a lengthy allegorical discussion regarding the purity of wine versus water, specifically referencing 'Cananaea' and 'Lyaei', and concludes with a poetic description of a garden and a warning against 'Talpas' (moles).

The text contains a series of poetic and didactic reflections on friendship (De Amicitia), the virtues of shared purpose, and the dangers of impulsive passion. It includes a formal congratulatory address (Ad Amicum Gratulatio) to a friend, referencing figures like Pyladen, Theseus, and Castor, and mentions the Muses and the poet Pindar. The final section features a series of short, allegorical, or satirical fragments involving biblical and mythological references, including Moses, Christ, and the Garamantes.

This section of the elegies contains a series of religious and allegorical poems. It includes a lament for a 'senex' (old man) and a series of exhortations to the 'Miles Christianus' (Christian Soldier) to remain steadfast against the 'Sathanicus' and the 'Colubrum Adamidis'. The final portion features a hymn of praise to peace and a concluding passage on the 'immaturi' (unripe/unprepared) death.

This section contains a series of religious and devotional poems or meditations, including a 'PERSEVERANDUM IN' prayer and a 'PERICULOSA VERBI' warning. The text features theological reflections on the resurrection of Christ, the fall of Adam, and the triumph over death, interspersed with liturgical-style exhortations and a concluding passage attributed to the Bishop of St. Basil.

This section contains a series of poetic and didactic passages, including a hymn to the Church (De Ecclesia) and a warning to a prince (Ad Principem Paraenis). It features references to biblical and mythological figures such as David, Solomon, Midas, and Apollo, and describes a diverse gathering of nations including Phoenicians and Indians at Zion. The text also includes a passage regarding the Temple of Peace in Rome and a concluding section titled 'Solomon's Youth'.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and a New Year's address. It features a moralizing exhortation to youth (pubes) to avoid the fleeting pleasures of the body and the 'cyclopean' excesses of lust, followed by a transition to a religious and commemorative section. The latter part includes a dedication to Hugo and Maxendies, mentions of figures like Christ, and a commemorative list of names and locations such as Sithonia and Idalia.

This section contains a series of elegies and carmina featuring several distinct dedications and poetic sequences. It includes a funerary or commemorative passage for 'Hildebrandus' and 'Georgius' involving themes of death, the afterlife, and the 'Book of Life,' followed by a 'Natalis Poetae' (Poet's Birthday) and a 'Guillemo Hildenio' sequence. The text concludes with a 'Dedicatoria' addressing 'Virtus' and 'Erato' regarding the nature of poetic craft and sacred severity.

This section of the 'Carminum' contains a hymn to the angels (De Angelis Hymnus) and a series of allegorical or mythological verses. It features a celestial and martial narrative involving figures such as Michael, Lucifer, and Cacus, and describes a spiritual conflict between holy orders and demonic forces. The text includes references to various entities like the 'Sanguinis', 'Pharmaca', and 'Mancipi', set against a backdrop of divine judgment and celestial protection.

This section contains a series of distinct poetic and dedicatory texts. It includes a religious allegory involving a 'Redeemer' and a 'multicephalous beast,' a dedication to a 'Baron' and 'Pector,' a formal dedication to 'Johann Rucard' (a physician and poet), and a celebratory panegyric for the 'Augustus' (Elector of Saxony) regarding the establishment of peace and the spread of the Christian faith.

This section contains a series of dedicatory and commemorative poems. It includes a praise of a poet named Elias Huter, a celebratory poem for a marriage (IN MATRIMONII), a dedication to a new spouse (PRO NOVIS CONIUGIBUS), a celebratory poem for a poet (PROPEMPTICUM), and a funeral elegy for Christoph Roeberstorfer of Vienna. The text also includes a final dedication to a poet (AD POETAM).

The text contains a series of religious and allegorical poems, including a section of 'Carminum' and an 'Elegia' (Elegia I). The content features a transition from a description of the Republic and the figure of Sophia to a series of prayers and meditations involving Christ, the figure of Moses, and the 'Aquila' (Eagle) as a symbol of the Church. The final section includes a polemical defense of the faith against 'Mahometis' (Muhammad) and a call to arms against an 'invisa gente' (invaded people).

This section contains a series of elegies and a dedicatory note. The text includes a passage on the 'Ship of the Church' (Navicula Ecclesiae) and a poem titled 'The Justice of the Exiles' (Justitia Exulans) which references figures such as Venus, Bacchus, and Niobe, as well as the laws of Sparta and the names of Aeacus, Minos, and Rhadamanthus. The final elegy is a prayer or address to a divine protector or 'Angel' regarding the poet's status and the service of the Lord.

This section contains a series of elegies and an epitaph featuring mythological and religious imagery. It includes a passage titled 'De Puperra ex Apocalypsi' referencing Apollo, the Moon, and the Apocalypse, and a section titled 'De Tyrannorum Insanid' involving the rivers Ister and Albis. The final section, 'Epitaphium Albi Submersorum,' describes a maritime disaster involving a ship and a figure named Festus.

The text contains a series of elegies and poems, including a section on a 'Good Shepherd' (Bonus Pastor) and a dedication to Henry Nicard, Secretary of the Military Courts. The poems feature mythological and pastoral imagery, referencing figures like Apollo, Admetus, and Venus (Cypria), and locations such as Hybla and Enna. The final section includes a dedication to a 'Nicarde' and a series of verses involving floral and pastoral metaphors.

This section of the elegies contains a series of pastoral and mythological verses featuring figures such as Philabella, Philomela, and Venus. The text describes a transition from winter to a blooming spring, invoking the goddess Ceres and the deity Phoebus, while incorporating imagery of gardens, vineyards, and birds. It concludes with a transition toward a more celestial focus on a man whose head is 'filled with stars' and who moves the paths of the heavens.

The text contains a series of poems, including a section of 'Carminum' and 'Elegiarum' (Elegies). The passages feature a mix of mythological and natural imagery, including references to Phoebe, the Temple of Solomon, and the figure of Adam. The final section, Elegia X, is a lament for a son named Elia, mentioning his parents, the loss of a daughter named Anna, and a final reference to the Danube (Ister) and the Austrian court.

The text contains two elegies (XI and XII) and a dedicatory note to a physician, Andreas Eberstorffer. Elegia XI features a dedication to the 'symbolum' of Nicolai Reicheli and reflects on themes of fate, divine will, and the struggle of the soul against adversity. Elegia XII contains a more complex, metaphorical meditation on physical suffering, the nature of pain, and the role of the poet.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses featuring a mixture of mythological, medical, and geographical imagery. It mentions specific locations such as Hesperia, Idalia, Cyprus, and Prague, and references figures or entities like Efferus, Gazula, and the goddess Trux. The passage contains heavy medical and physical imagery involving 'podagra' (gout), 'morbus' (disease), and 'crura' (legs/feet), alongside references to horses, chariots, and a 'shepherdess' of a flock.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses describing a grim, allegorical landscape of disease, physical suffering, and medical treatment. It mentions mythological figures such as Pluto, Tisiphone, Apollo, and the Eumenides, alongside geographical and cultural references like the River Norica, the Graeae, and the city of Rome. The passage also references specific names like Eberstorff, Titius, and the physician-like role of the poet, while describing the preparation of medicinal mixtures and the physical toll of illness.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and a concluding medical dedication to Dr. Eberstorfer. The poems contain a mix of mythological imagery (Apollo, Jove, Ganymede), geographical references (Dresden, Lipsia, the river Silesus), and medical descriptions involving ailments like gout (podagra) and the preparation of medicinal herbs. The final section explicitly praises the medical skills and pharmacological knowledge of the physician Eberstorfer.

The text contains a series of Latin poems, including a section of 'Carminum' and 'Elegiarum' and a specific 'Elegia XV' regarding Austrian thermal springs (Thermae Austriacae). The passages mention figures such as Delius, Chiron, and the author Abel, while referencing medical themes, the healing properties of mineral waters, and the fertility of women. A specific mention of 'D. Eberstorff' appears in the context of the thermal springs.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and a formal dedication to 'Augustino a Lidlau'. It features a celebratory section involving figures such as Lidelius, Judith, and Eberstorferus, and includes a drinking song (Elegia XVI) with references to the Muses, the river Ister, and the deity Portunum. The final section transitions into a religious meditation on Christ, the redemption of the Jewish people, and the dangers of the Danube.

The text begins with a religious meditation on salvation, divine mercy, and the suffering of the faithful. It transitions into a mock-heroic or satirical epigram featuring a lion, an ass, and a rooster in a comedic confrontation. The final section is a dedicated elegy to D. Christophorus Pelargus, describing a maritime voyage involving mythical and geographical references such as the Isthmus of Grai, the city of Rostoch, and the lands of the Pomeranians.

The text transitions from a maritime voyage and a journey toward the East, mentioning the Euphrates, the Aegean, and the conversion of the Gentiles. It features a shift to a medical narrative where the speaker describes suffering from a severe illness (rheum, cough, and asthma) and the subsequent administration of medicines and wine by physicians.

The text is a series of elegiac verses containing a mix of pastoral imagery, mythological references, and personal dedications. It mentions specific figures such as Bacchus, Apollo, and several individuals with German-sounding names (Schraderus, Haslobius, Cornerus, Copernicus). The passage describes landscapes involving the Rhine, the Alps (Lycaeus), and various vineyards, while also referencing historical or literary figures like Aonius and the poeter Sabinus.

This section contains a series of elegies and dedications. It includes a poem dedicated to the Queen of England regarding the constellation Cassiopeia, a memorial for the physician Petrus Monavius (referred to as 'D. Petri Monavii'), and a formal address to Jacob Colerum in Berlin. The text mentions several mythological figures such as Tritoniger, Dionysus, and Perseus, and references geographical locations like Britain, Italy, and the city of Berlin.

The text contains a series of elegiac verses and poems featuring several named figures, including Haslobius, Marchia, and the poet Fabricius. It contains personal reflections on the hardships of life, the preservation of literary works, and the enduring fame of certain authors. The passage also mentions specific locations and entities such as the Aonii fountain, the land of Gaul, and the court of Pollio.

This section contains a series of elegies and a funerary inscription (Epitaphium) featuring names such as Dimidius, Colere, and Haslobius. The text includes a dedication to the study of sacred scriptures and languages, and a specific elegy (Elegia V) referencing geographical and mythological locations like the Hyperborean lands, the land of the Saxons, and the city of Martigene. The passage also mentions figures such as Pallas, Solomon, and Pierius, while referencing themes of divine mystery, poetic fame, and the preservation of ancient traditions.

This section of the 'Carminum' contains a series of lyrical and mythological verses featuring figures such as Mathusalah, Apollo, Minerva, and various deities like Ceres, Nereus, and Faunus. The text describes pastoral and sacred landscapes, including the Hesperides, the Garden of Hesperides, and the lands of Enna and Hybla, while referencing mythological locations like the Lyceum and the shores of the sea. It concludes with a series of invocations and descriptions of divine grace and musical performance.

The text contains a series of Latin poems, including a section of odes and a dedicated elegy (Elegia VI) addressed to Abraham Risen, a mathematician. The poems feature mythological and geographical references including Chloris, the mountains of Orea, the Borean realm, and the Isthmus of Cymbricus. The final section addresses the recipient's mathematical expertise, referencing Pallas, Pythagoras, and the geometry of the sphere.

The text contains a series of poetic and didactic reflections, including a formal address to 'Eliam Hutterum' regarding works in Dresden and the study of the Bible. It features a scholarly defense of scholarly labor, the preservation of ancient languages, and the distinction between profound scholarship and 'vulgar' usage. The passage mentions specific figures or entities such as Elia, Thamirac, Tiresias, and the city of Fulgida.

The text contains a series of elegies (Elegia VIII and IX) and a concluding section of a larger work. The passages feature religious and allegorical imagery involving the Gospel, the Eucharist, and the transition from 'piety' to 'religion,' while also incorporating classical and mythological references such as Ulysses, Aeneas (Atrides), and the city of Pergamum. The text concludes with a dedication to Andreas Reussius and includes specific mentions of the names Reussius and Vulnificus.
The text contains a single line of verse regarding the construction of eternal monuments. It references a 'Caesar' who has bestowed favor upon a recipient as a reward for wisdom.

This work is a liturgical collection for the feast of Saint Domnius, provided in an electronic version by Adam Parižanin. The text is organized into three distinct sections containing chants, hagiography, and ritual instructions. The first section contains antiphons, psalms, and a hagiographic narrative (Passio) concerning the Syrian noble Theodosius and his son Dompnius. The second section provides readings, responses, and verses featuring figures such as Antiocenis, Maurilius, and Beatus Petrus, with specific references to the regions of Dalmatia and Salona. The final section contains musical instructions for the Secundis Vesperis, a hymn to the Trinity, and an antiphona for the Magnificat mentioning the 'Corpora sanctorum' and Masarontis.

This text contains a series of liturgical chants, antiphons, and psalms for the feast of Saint Domnius (S. Domnii). It includes a hagiographic narrative (Passio) detailing the life of Theodosius, a Syrian man of noble birth, and his son Dompnius, who is portrayed as a martyr and teacher of the faith.

This section of the liturgical text contains a series of readings (Lectio), responses (Responsorium), and verses (Versiculus) for a feast, likely related to Saint Domnius. It features several specific figures including the figures of Antiochus (Antiocenis), Maurilius, and the 'Blessed Peter' (Beatus Petrus). The text includes liturgical movements involving the cities of Dalmatia and Salon, and references to the martyrdom of a soldier-like figure and the defense of the faith.

This section contains liturgical verses and a musical instruction for the 'Secundis Vesperis'. The text includes a hymn to the 'Sublimi Domino' regarding the Trinity and the crowning of saints, and a specific antiphona for the Magnificat involving the 'Corpora sanctorum' and a reference to 'Masarontis'.

This document is a Latin charter of land and vineyard donation dated 1070. The donor, Radauanus, grants his possessions, which were previously held by his ancestor Ualeco, to the monastery of Saint Chrysogon. The text identifies the reigning authorities as the third Roman Emperor and King Peter of Croatia and Dalmatia. The transaction is recorded in the city of Nona Adamizo. A list of thirteen witnesses is provided, including several individuals with the title 'iupano' and several priests. The document concludes with a standard ecclesiastical curse against those who would tamper with the charter and a closing certification by Adam, a priest and monk.

This collection consists of three hymns and a series of liturgical texts (hymns, antiphons, and prayers) dedicated to the martyr and pontiff Saint Domnius. The work is organized into five parts that detail the liturgical history, hagiography, and translation of the saint's relics in the diocese of Spalatum (Split) and the city of Salona. The text includes specific references to the province of Dalmatia and the island of Diomedes. Liturgical components include offices for Vespers, Matins, and the Easter season, as well as a Magnificat. The content features invocations for protection against the 'monstra Tartari' (Turks) and prayers against disease and famine. The text also includes a hagiographical account involving Saint John of Fulginus and mentions of a figure named Maurilius.

The text begins with a historical and liturgical introduction regarding the translation of the relics of Saint Domnius (S. Domnius) in the diocese of Split (Spalatum) and the celebration of his feast. It notes the history of three previous translations and the establishment of a unified feast day on the Kalends of August. The section concludes with three hymns (Hymni) dedicated to Saint Domnius, featuring poetic praises of his martyrdom, the triumph over paganism, and the celestial glory of the Trinity.

This section contains a series of liturgical hymns, antiphons, and psalms for the feast of a martyr named Domnius (or Domnius). The text includes references to the city of Salona (Solana), the province of Dalmatia, and a specific narrative involving a figure named Maurilius and a conflict with the 'monstra Tartari'.

This section contains liturgical texts (hymns, antiphons, and prayers) for the veneration of Saint Domnius, a martyr and pontiff associated with the city of Spalatum (modern-day Split). The text includes specific references to the city's status as the 'First Metropolis,' the physical attributes of the saint's sarcophagus, and his role as a protector of the local people. The liturgical structure includes sections for Vespers, Matins, and the Easter season.

This section contains liturgical texts (hymns, antiphons, and prayers) for the feast of Saint Domnius, a martyr and bishop (Pontifex) from Salona (modern-day Solin, Croatia). The text includes specific invocations for protection against the Turks, prayers for the remission of diseases and famine, and mentions of the region of Dalmatia.

This section contains liturgical texts for the feast of Saint Domnius, including a hymn and various prayers for the evening and morning offices. It includes a historical and hagiographical account of Saint Domnius and Saint John of Fulginus, mentioning the city of Spalatum (Split) and the island of Diomedes. The text also references the translation of the saints' bodies and the influence of the Benedictine monastery.

This Latin text, 'Commentarius rerum actarum Constantinopoli anno 1542', is a diplomatic report and record of negotiations concerning the Ottoman Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary. The work is organized into seven sections detailing the author's journey through Dalmatia and Messia, his meetings with Ottoman officials such as Rustam Bassa, Solimano Bassa, and the eunuch counselor of Sultan Suleiman. It documents specific negotiations regarding the cession of Buda and four fortresses (Strigonium, Vissegrad, Tattam, and Alba Regalis) in exchange for annual payments of 50,000 gold pieces or ducats. The text includes diplomatic exchanges involving the Holy Roman Empire, the Venetian Republic, and the Polish King. Key geographical locations mentioned include Vienna, Galata, Pest, Belgrade, and Adrianople. The narrative also references historical figures such as Maximilian, Ladislaus, and Sigismund, while discussing military movements and the status of various envoys.

The text is a report by a diplomat (likely a representative of the Holy Roman Empire) regarding his journey to Constantinople in 1542. It details the hardships of the journey through Dalmatia and Messia, the observation of the Turkish military's state of exhaustion, and a diplomatic meeting with the eunuch and first counselor of Sultan Suleiman. The author argues for the pursuit of peace over the uncertainty of military victory, citing the fragility of human power.

The text records a diplomatic negotiation regarding the Kingdom of Hungary and the city of Buda. The author, acting as a formal envoy (legatus), argues for the peaceful transfer of Buda and four specific fortresses (Strigonium, Vissegrad, Tattam, and Alba Regalis) from the Emperor to his master. The passage includes a debate over the author's status as a diplomat versus an explorer and mentions a specific offer of 50,000 gold pieces annually for the maintenance of the territory.

The narrator recounts a diplomatic encounter with the Ottoman officials Mechmet and Usrei, and later with Rustam Bassa, regarding the capture and execution of a servant who was an expert in the Turkish language. The text details a subsequent meeting with Sultan Soliman, where the narrator discusses the status of the Kingdom of Hungary, the defense of Buda, and the actions of Jonus Beg. The narrative includes specific geographical references to Vienna, Buda, and Galata, and mentions historical figures such as Maximilian, Ladislaus, and Sigismund.

The text contains a diplomatic petition from a royal envoy to the Emperor (referred to as 'V. Imperial Alteza') regarding the Kingdom of Hungary and the city of Buda. The envoy argues that the King of Hungary (the 'Re mio ser.mo') seeks the Emperor's favor and generosity to secure the region, framing the Emperor's potential concession as an act of immense glory and a means to establish lasting peace in Europe. The document includes a specific offer of 50,000 Hungarian ducats annually in exchange for the cession of Buda and the Hungarian kingdom.
